episode_title: Paulien Cornelisse, 1950s-style border checks end, and a box 3 revolt
description: The Netherlands mourns Paulien Cornelisse, the writer and comedian who made the country laugh at its own language. MPs push back on taxing small savers, mortgage rates hit a yearly high, and prosecutors get tougher on attacks on public workers. Plus a $180 million Van Gogh, the price of a TikTok chip queue, and what's on in Amsterdam this weekend.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands has lost one of its sharpest, funniest observers of its own language. Paulien Cornelisse has died at fifty, while she was still on TV every night.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And in The Hague, MPs push back on a plan that would tax hundreds of thousands of small savers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Thursday, the first of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm Sam, and this is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We begin with the death of Paulien Cornelisse, the writer and comedian.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: She died of cancer yesterday at Amsterdam's Antoni van Leeuwenhoek hospital, with her loved ones there. She was fifty, and had been diagnosed in 2024.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sam, for anyone who's new here, who was she?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Think of a national language-watcher with a comedian's timing. She broke through in 2009 with a bestseller called Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding. Roughly: 'Language is, like, totally my thing.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The title's the joke and the thesis at the same time.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Exactly. She picked apart everyday Dutch. Filler words, office jargon, the things people say without meaning them. It sold seven hundred thousand copies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And last year, her essay for national Book Week, about common Dutch words, sold out on day two. That had never happened before.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But most people knew her from TV. She was the one-person jury on De Slimste Mens, 'The Smartest Person', a quiz that's on every weeknight.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And people saw her there every night, right until this week. The episodes were recorded before the summer, while she was on chemo. She wore a hat or a cap in every one, because she'd lost her hair and didn't want a wig.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The broadcaster, KRO-NCRV, spoke with her family and dropped last night's episode. The rest move back a day, with new dates to come.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: She was also about to return to the stage, with a new show at Amsterdam's DeLaMar theatre called Waar was ik gebleven. 'Where was I.' It's been cancelled, and ticket holders will get refunds.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Prime Minister Rob Jetten called her 'sharp, funny and incredibly kind.' Her co-host Herman van der Zandt said that even between treatments she was 'wonderfully energetic.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Her last column for de Volkskrant ran just a week ago. She was puzzling over apegapen, a Dutch word for being utterly exhausted.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Still turning words over, one week before she died.

segments.title: Border checks end, wider spot checks begin

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, the borders with Belgium and Germany, where the checks have ended. Sort of.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sort of?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Since December 2024, the Koninklijke Marechaussee, the military police who guard the borders, has run temporary checks at the land crossings. They were brought in by Marjolein Faber, the asylum minister from Geert Wilders' PVV. As of yesterday, they're over.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In the Schengen area there are normally no passport checks between countries. You can bring them back, but only temporarily, and you have to justify it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The current minister, Bart van den Brink, calls this a policy choice. Border towns and businesses had complained about the traffic jams. Up to March this year, about six hundred people were refused entry, mostly for lacking valid papers, and two hundred and seventy were arrested for things like smuggling.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here's the twist, though. From today, the Marechaussee goes back to spot checks anywhere within twenty kilometres of the border. But with more room. More hours on the same road, and no six-hour daily limit.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And on a selected train, every passenger can now be checked. Same for selected flights from other Schengen countries, though only up to a quarter of them on any route.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Marechaussee says smugglers can no longer count on a checkpoint packing up after six hours. And Germany is keeping its own border checks until at least next March.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So fewer queues at the crossing, but maybe a spot check down the road.

segments.title: MPs balk at taxing small savers

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Your savings now, and a tax plan that's already wobbling in The Hague.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yesterday we told you the cabinet wants to cut the tax-free return in box 3, the tax on savings and investments, to a thousand euros. About eight hundred and fifty thousand more people would pay.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On day one of the annual budget debate in the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, that ran into a wall.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA has no majority, so it needs opposition votes. JA21, ChristenUnie, the SGP and Pro are all against. The SGP called it 'a fine on thrift'.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the coalition itself?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Wobbling. The CDA called it 'an unfortunate point'. D66 says it'll look at serious alternatives, but only ones that raise the same money from taxing wealth. That's about four hundred and seventy million euros. No concrete alternative yet.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And savers face another squeeze first. For 2027, the cabinet wants to roughly halve today's tax-free allowance, to about thirty-one thousand euros per person. That still needs both houses to pass it by the end of the year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Income tax is the other fight. Both bands go up next year, only partly offset by a bigger work tax credit. The Council of State, the government's top legal adviser, noted that almost all of the six billion in extra taxes lands on workers.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: BBB's Vermeer called it 'taking two hundred euros, giving back a hundred and expecting you to be happy.' JA21 and Pro want that rise scaled back before they'll back the cabinet.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's friction over that fallback education cut, too. D66 brushed it off as the work of an 'overzealous civil servant'. But the VVD confirmed it's the agreed plan B.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Finance Minister Heinen responds today. If you've got savings, keep an eye on this one.

segments.title: Mortgage rates peak as estate agents face a register

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Staying with money: mortgage rates have hit their highest level this year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The average ten-year fixed rate with NHG, the National Mortgage Guarantee, is now four and a half percent. In late August it was just over four. NHG is government backing for homes below a set price, and it gets you a lower rate.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And here, how much you can borrow is tied directly to the rate. Take a couple earning ninety thousand a year. At three and a half percent, they could borrow about four hundred and thirteen thousand euros. Now, about three hundred and ninety-five.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why's it climbing? Is that the European Central Bank?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Mostly not. The ECB has held its rate. It's the capital markets, where banks raise money, driven by worries about inflation, energy prices and geopolitical tension.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So do house prices finally come down?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not yet. Demand still far outstrips supply. But Amsterdam is cooling. In the second quarter, prices here were less than one percent higher than a year earlier. Nationally, it was over four. ABN Amro expects that cooling to spread.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meanwhile, Housing Minister Boekholt-O'Sullivan is going after estate agents, the makelaars. Right now, you don't need any government licence to be one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's changing. Every agent will have to be on a government register, with a complaints desk and a disputes committee that can strike rogue agents off.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And here's the big one for buyers. Agents will have to show you the biedlogboek, the bidding log.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That matters, because Dutch bidding is blind. People often bid way over asking without knowing what anyone else offered.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Concrete plans are due early next year. Until then, it's still bidding in the dark.

segments.title: Prison as the default for attacks on public workers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tougher punishment now for anyone who attacks people working for the public.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meaning police officers?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And many more: paramedics, train staff, teachers, referees, judges, journalists. From today, a new guideline from the Openbaar Ministerie, the prosecution service, says every attack on them goes to court. No settling it with a fine or community service.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And what will prosecutors ask for?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Double the usual sentence, with prison as the starting point. The justice minister gave an example. A first offender attempts a serious assault on a paramedic. No weapon, no injury. Against an ordinary person, that's eighty hours of community service. Against the paramedic, prosecutors would now ask for three months in prison.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So, not automatic jail.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No, judges still decide. This follows New Year's Eve, when police and firefighters were attacked, sometimes lured into ambushes.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Same day, rail staff sounded the alarm. Their union, VVMC, says NS, the national railway, has logged over five thousand reports of aggression against staff this year. In all of 2023, it was under three thousand.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Including conductors knocked unconscious, and one employee badly bitten on the thumb during an arrest.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The union wants more security staff on trains. And it wants back the powers senior conductors lost in 2022, when NS dropped them to save money. Since then, they can't write official reports or check someone's details in the population register.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: NS says it shares the concerns, and it's giving every conductor a body camera.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And on the line between Zwolle and Emmen, operator Arriva has told staff to let threatening fare dodgers go, rather than wait around twenty-five minutes for police.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The union's answer: more security on the trains, not letting people walk.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here in Amsterdam, a trial treating crack addiction with medication has been abruptly halted.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The idea was a bit like methadone for heroin users. Give crack users a controlled stimulant, dexamphetamine, normally an ADHD drug, to reduce their cravings.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So who stopped it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The IGJ, the national health inspectorate. It halted production of the medicine at a hospital it won't name, saying it's concerned about the medicine's quality. It hasn't said what those concerns are.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And people were already taking it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. The first participants had already started, and their treatment's been interrupted. Alderman Alexander Scholtes couldn't say how many people are affected.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Scholtes, the city's alderman for health, called it 'the only promising method' for people with heavy addictions. He and Mayor Femke Halsema asked Health Minister Sophie Hermans to review the decision and bring everyone together before November.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Has she?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: She's replied, but made no promise of a meeting. She said she understands the concerns, but the inspectorate is independent. Quote, 'I have confidence in their judgment.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The city health service estimates there are between three and nine thousand crack users in Amsterdam, many of them homeless. The research team has until the end of the year to decide whether the study can go on.

segments.title: The Netherlands threatens to withhold money from Italy

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Back to asylum minister Bart van den Brink, who's now threatening to withhold money from Italy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Some background. Under the EU's Dublin rules, the country where an asylum seeker first enters the EU is usually responsible for them. Other countries can send people back there.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Italy, where many people arrive across the Mediterranean, has for years largely refused to take them back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In June, the two countries agreed transfers would resume. In practice, very little has happened. In the first three weeks of the new EU Migration Pact, Italy carried out none of the twelve transfer requests it got from EU countries.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Dutch courts keep blocking transfers, too. On the twenty-second of September, judges ruled in three cases that the minister hadn't shown Italy had reception places set aside.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now the money. Under the pact, countries either take in asylum seekers from places like Italy, or pay. The Netherlands chose to pay. Its share of the EU pot this year is about eleven million euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Van den Brink told parliament yesterday: 'If something doesn't work, we won't pay.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He plans to take that message to other EU ministers and the European Commission.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, have you got a spare hundred and eighty million dollars?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Let me check the couch cushions. Why?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's what Sotheby's expects for Van Gogh's Chestnut Trees in Blossom, up for auction in New York in November. It says it could top two hundred million.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That would smash his auction record, a hundred and seventeen million dollars.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He painted it in May 1890, just outside Paris, two months before he died. It hasn't been shown in public since 1964.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Good news, then: the Van Gogh Museum is still the cheaper ticket.

segments.title: The price of a TikTok chip queue

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Back to Fabel Friet, the TikTok-famous chip shop in the Nine Streets.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Neighbours are already in court over its queues. Now a TU Delft researcher has put a price on them.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Homes within five hundred metres sold for nearly five percent less than similar ones further away, about forty-one thousand euros. Within seventy metres, more than eleven percent.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Forty-one thousand euros. For fries.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Caveat: the queues only began in 2022, late in the study period, and it doesn't pin down the cause.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And a Het Parool opinion piece told the complainers they're 'warmly welcome in Purmerend.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: If you'd rather queue for something free, Saturday's got you covered.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: IJver, up at the NDSM Wharf in Amsterdam-Noord, is throwing an anniversary party from four till nine. A thousand free oysters, a thousand free bitterballen, and cheap beer and spritz. Free entry, no sign-up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Free food while it lasts, so don't stroll in at half eight.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Fair. What's yours?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Joe Hisaishi, the composer behind the Studio Ghibli films, conducting the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost, Friday through Sunday. Spirited Away, Ponyo, Howl's Moving Castle, with film clips on a big screen. And he plays piano himself.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm going to cry, and I'm fine with that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Just check the date. The orchestra's also doing a Beethoven's Ninth night there, so don't book the wrong one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: For art, Chez Matisse opens Saturday at the H'ART Museum in the Plantage. More than eighty works, including La Blouse roumaine, and it's on until mid-February.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From tonight through Saturday, there's the Afrovibes Festival at De Brakke Grond in the city centre, starting around half seven. Dance, theatre, music and spoken word by artists from Africa and the diaspora, on land, ancestry and belonging. It also hits the Bijlmer Parktheater and Framer Framed this weekend, though those dates may still shift.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And on Sunday, the market at Westergas in Westerpark. Street food, local makers, art. Pair it with a walk in the park.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Dutch Daily Briefing for Thursday. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. Thanks for listening, see you tomorrow.
